sections.title: Biography
sections.html:
Before she painted, Alexandra Johnson worked as a trader. She has described that world as hard, fast and short on feeling, and has said she is a gentler person now.[ap-muse]

The turn came with the death of her mother, to whom she was very close. In interview she links that loss directly to the determination that drove her into painting, working under the name Zara Muse.[ap-muse]

Her portraits have since been hung in luxury hotels, including sites run by the Fairmont group, and in Kanishka, a restaurant in Mayfair. Limited edition prints followed, to bring the work to a wider audience, and collectors in Dubai have begun to buy it.[lno-muse]

I want to champion and support women.Zara Muse, speaking to Luxury News Online, 2025[lno-muse]

Her gallery adds two details we have not been able to check elsewhere, so we give them as the gallery's account: that she has made art since childhood and spent her summer holidays doing so, and that she is the cousin of a well-known street artist. Reported[grove-zm]

sections.title: Style and technique
sections.html:
Zara Muse paints only with palette knives and spatulas, never brushes. She has called the choice instinctive, made for the depth and richness it gives the surface.[ap-muse]

The result is paint that stands proud of the canvas. Colour is laid in thick, flat-edged slabs rather than blended, so a cheek or a jawline is built from separate planes of saturated colour. Seen close up the face breaks into ridges; from across a room it comes back together.

Her subjects are women, and she has said she wants the work to celebrate the strength and resilience of the women in her own life, her mother included.[lno-muse] Many of the titles are Spanish: Bella Dama del Sol, Luz Serena, Viento del Sur. The gallery describes the work as exploring nature, emotion and human connection through a rich palette.[grove-port][grove-zm]

How to read one

Start with the lit side of the face, where the slabs are thickest and most separate. Count the planes that make the cheek. Then find the shadow side, where she tends to let the knife drag one colour through another. The join between the two is where the portrait either holds together or does not, and in the strongest works it is left slightly unresolved, so the eye keeps working at it.

Read moreUnderstanding palette-knife painting
The role of texture in contemporary portraiture

artists.name: Konn Artiss
artists.summary: An unnamed artist, or collective, staging public interventions in Venice, Washington and London that question money, fame and the art market.
artists.dek: Nobody has said publicly who Konn Artiss is. What we can document is the work: short-lived, theatrical interventions that turn the money and celebrity around art into the subject of the art itself.
artists.heroCredit: Image: ANTI-FRIEZE, London, October 2025. Courtesy Konn Artiss
glance: Anonymous. Reported both as a single artist and as a collective
Installation, effigies, ice, printed matter, staged demonstrations

sections.title: Who is Konn Artiss?
sections.html:
The honest answer is that no one has said. Reports differ even on whether Konn Artiss is one person: The Art Newspaper describes an art collective, while other coverage calls it a single mysterious artist and notes that both theories are in circulation.[tan-frieze][fad-ghost]

Anonymity is part of the work. Interventions appear without warning in public space, are photographed and shared, and are gone within days. That pattern has built a mythology around the name, which is itself a subject the work keeps returning to: who gets famous, and why.[ap-antifrieze]

How we report this artistMuch of what is published about Konn Artiss starts with the project's own statements. Where a claim has not been confirmed by an independent source, we mark it Reported rather than state it as fact.

sections.title: Themes and approach
sections.html:
Three ideas run through the work so far: wealth and who controls public space, the art market's habit of turning names into prices, and the fragility of value itself.

The materials are chosen to make those points physical. Ice melts. A newspaper is read and thrown away. An effigy in a canal drifts out of view. The work is designed not to last, which is a pointed choice for an art world built on preserving and reselling objects.[ap-antifrieze]

Read moreMixed-media art: materials, meaning and conservation
Review: ANTI-FRIEZE

articles.title: Zara Muse: biography, artistic style and career
articles.dek: From a trading floor to the auction room. How a London painter built a body of sculptural, palette-knife portraits of women, and what to look for in the surface of the work.
articles.credit: Image: Zara Muse portrait, detail. Supplied by Grove Gallery
articles.body:
Some artists arrive through art school, residencies and group shows. Zara Muse arrived from the City. Before she picked up a palette knife, Alexandra Johnson was a trader, in a job she has described as intense and, looking back, soulless.[ap-muse] The paintings she makes now could hardly be further from it: slow, physical, built up by hand, layer on layer.

A change of direction

The change was not planned. Johnson has spoken openly about the death of her mother, to whom she was very close, and about how the grief that followed left her stronger and more determined.[ap-muse] Painting became the place that determination went. She took the name Zara Muse for the work.

That story matters for how we read the paintings. Her subjects are women, and she has said plainly that she wants the work to stand for the strength and resilience she saw in her mother, in herself and in the women around her.[lno-muse]

Knives, not brushes

The most distinctive thing about a Zara Muse painting is how it is made. She works only with palette knives and spatulas, never brushes, a choice she has described as instinctive.[ap-muse] The acrylic goes on thick and is pushed into shape rather than stroked, so each passage of colour keeps a hard edge where the knife lifted away.

Look closely and you see the method. Skin is not blended into soft gradients; it is built from separate, flat planes of strong colour laid side by side. The eye does the blending, which is why the portraits seem to sharpen as you step back from them. The paint has real height, so the way a work is lit changes what you see. A light from the side throws every ridge into shadow.

What to look forStand close, then far. Close up, notice where the knife has dragged one colour through another, and where a fresh, untouched slab sits on top. Far away, notice how few of those slabs it takes to make a convincing face.

From walls to the saleroom

The work found its first wide audience on hospitality walls rather than in museums. Her portraits have hung in luxury hotels, including Fairmont group sites, and in Kanishka in Mayfair, and limited edition prints were introduced so that more people could own one.[lno-muse] The same profile reports the work reaching collectors in Dubai.[lno-muse]

The most widely reported moment came at auction. Her portrait of Malala Yousafzai sold at Bonhams for £51,000. She has said she chose Malala because she sees in her the resilience and courage the work sets out to celebrate.[ap-muse] Her paintings have also passed through the London auction house Tate Ward.[ap-muse]

Reading the career so far

For a collector or a curious reader, a few things are worth holding together. The technique is consistent and recognisable, which is rarer than it sounds. The subject matter is focused. And the career has moved quickly, through commercial interiors and prints as much as through exhibitions. A single strong auction result is a meaningful moment, but it is one data point; the more useful question is how the work develops from here.

Zara Muse is represented by Grove Gallery, which released a new print collection on 4 November 2026.[grove]

articles.title: Konn Artiss: artist profile and selected works
articles.dek: An anonymous name, a sign-off that reads Trust Me, and a run of interventions that put the art market on ice. What we know, what is only reported, and why it matters.
articles.credit: Image: ANTI-FRIEZE, London, 2025. Courtesy Konn Artiss
articles.body:
In the summer of 2025 a name began to appear around stunts aimed at the very rich. By the autumn it had turned up outside the biggest art fair in London. The name was Konn Artiss, and the sign-off attached to it was Trust Me.[fad-ghost]

A name without a face

Nobody has publicly identified who is behind Konn Artiss, and even the basic question of whether it is one person is unsettled. Some coverage describes a single anonymous street artist; The Art Newspaper describes an elusive collective.[fad-ghost][tan-frieze] We use "the artist" in this profile for simplicity, without taking a side.

Selected works

The Washington Ghost, Venice, 2025

Ahead of Jeff Bezos's wedding in Venice, more than 10,000 copies of a satirical newspaper called The Washington Ghost were handed out in the city. Around the same time a mannequin of Bezos was floated through the canals.[gb-venice] The newspaper is the more interesting object: a work that looks like journalism, is given away free, and is meant to be read and thrown away.

The same project ran a staged demonstration in Washington DC. FAD Magazine also reports that work connected to The Washington Ghost was displayed three times at the National Portrait Gallery, including in the room where presidential portraits hang.[fad-ghost] We have not been able to confirm that independently, so we mark it as reported.

ANTI-FRIEZE, London, 2025

During Frieze week, five large blocks of ice appeared outside Frieze London, each holding an effigy of a famous artist: Damien Hirst, Andy Warhol, Tracey Emin, Jeff Koons and KAWS.[ap-antifrieze] Over the following days the ice melted, leaving puddles and debris.

The Art Newspaper also reported blocks of ice placed outside major London galleries and auction houses that week, including a framed image taped to the window at Phillips alongside a block of ice, with the artist comparing the frame to the market's context and the ice to its reality.[tan-frieze]

Reading the workEach piece turns a symbol of permanence into something temporary. Famous names are frozen, like assets kept in storage, and then simply allowed to melt. The work asks what an artist's reputation is worth when nobody is preserving it.

Why it matters

Konn Artiss sits in a long line of artists who use anonymity and public space to criticise the institutions that sell art. What is different is the target: not just the powerful in general, but the art market's own celebrities and prices. Whether the project has staying power, and how it relates to any saleable work, is something we will keep documenting as it develops.

articles.title: Understanding palette-knife painting
articles.dek: What a knife does that a brush cannot, how painters use it, and how to read the ridges it leaves behind.
articles.body:
A palette knife was first a mixing tool: a thin, flexible blade for blending colours on the palette before they went anywhere near the canvas. At some point painters noticed that the knife could also put paint on, and that it left marks no brush could make.

Knife or brush: what changes

A brush holds paint in its bristles and releases it gradually, leaving fine grooves and soft, feathered edges. A knife carries paint on a flat steel surface and lays it down all at once. That gives three effects that define the technique:

  • Clean, hard edges. Where the blade lifts, the paint stops. Colours sit side by side rather than melting into each other.
  • Height. A knife can lay paint thickly and leave it standing. This thick paint is called impasto.
  • Flat, light-catching planes. The smooth underside of the blade presses the paint flat, so each stroke reflects light like a tiny facet.

The tools

Painting knives usually have a cranked handle, bent so that the knuckles clear the canvas, and come in many blade shapes: long and narrow for lines, broad trowels for covering ground, small pointed tips for detail. Some painters use spatulas or scrapers for the largest areas. The edge of the blade can also be dragged through wet paint to scratch back to the layer beneath, a technique called sgraffito.

Oil or acrylic

Knife painting works in both, but they behave differently. Thick oil paint can take a very long time to dry right through, and heavy layers need care to avoid cracking or wrinkling. Acrylic dries far faster, and heavy-body acrylics and gel mediums are made to hold a peak, which suits painters who build up many thick layers in a session. The trade-off is less time to move paint around before it sets.

A short history

In the nineteenth century, Gustave Courbet made the knife part of his signature. The Getty describes how, in a painting of a cave at Sarrazine, he applied and scraped off paint with a palette knife to mimic the cavern's coloured, textured surfaces, and it credits his landscapes of the 1860s with turning painting into a tactile performance in paint that the Impressionists and later painters would take up.[getty-courbet]

In the twentieth century, Nicolas de Staël built whole compositions from knifed colour. The Phillips Collection notes that much of his work of the 1940s is made of small geometric blocks with a heavy impasto applied with a palette knife,[phillips-destael] and the Thyssen describes a palette of ochres, browns, greys and blacks laid on with brushes and palette knives in very thick layers that construct space by colour alone.[thyssen-destael]

Many contemporary painters, including Zara Muse, use the knife for portraits, where it turns a face into a structure of coloured planes. Her gallery describes a technique combining palette knife and spatula that gives the work a three-dimensional quality.[grove-zm]

How to look at a knife painting

  1. Step back first. Knife paintings are often designed to resolve at a distance. See the image before you see the paint.
  2. Then step in. Find a single area, say a cheekbone, and count how many separate knife strokes make it.
  3. Look at the edges. Has one colour been dragged through another while wet, or laid on top after drying? That tells you the order the painting was made in.
  4. Move around it. Because the paint has height, the picture changes with the light. Look from the side as well as straight on.
Try itLook at any knife painting from the side, almost along the surface, with the room light behind you. The ridges will show their direction, and the direction of the strokes tells you how the painter's hand moved: down a cheek, round a jaw, across a background.

For the words used above, see A short glossary of paint; for the two paints in more detail, Oil or acrylic.

For collectorsThick paint photographs badly. Ask to see a knife painting in person, or ask for photographs lit from the side, which show the surface far better than a flat studio shot.

articles.title: The role of texture in contemporary portraiture
articles.dek: Why so many painters build faces up from the canvas instead of smoothing them flat, and what that surface is asking of the viewer.
articles.credit: Image: portrait surface, raking light. [Image to supply]
articles.body:
For centuries the ambition of portrait painting was, broadly, to make the paint disappear. A polished surface let the sitter's face come forward and the painter's hand fall away. Texture turns that around. It insists that what you are looking at is paint, put there by a person, and asks you to hold the face and the material in mind at once.

An old idea

Heavy paint in portraiture is not new. In his late self-portraits, Rembrandt built up the lit parts of the face in thick paint, so that the surface itself catches real light where the face catches painted light. The National Gallery of Art in Washington describes the thick impastos and bold strokes with which he modelled his own face in 1659,[nga-rembrandt] and pigment analysis of the London self-portrait of 1669 finds the thick impasto on the cheek to be lead white tinted with ochres, painted over a brown undermodelling.[colourlex-rembrandt] The structure is the same one a knife painter uses today: dark underneath, light built up on top.

In the twentieth century, Frank Auerbach painted and scraped his portraits of the same few sitters over and over. The National Galleries of Scotland note that although his paint appears to have accumulated over months, he regularly scraped it all off to start afresh,[ngs-auerbach] and Tate's conservators record him working with brushes, palette knives, putty scrapers and sometimes paint squeezed straight from the tube.[tate-auerbach] Each shows a different reason for texture: for Rembrandt, to make light physical; for Auerbach, to keep the record of looking.

What texture does today

It slows you down

A textured portrait cannot be taken in from a phone screen. It asks to be seen in a room, at different distances, and that slower looking is part of the experience.

It gives the sitter physical presence

When paint stands proud of the canvas, the portrait becomes an object as well as an image. Many painters use this to give their subjects weight and solidity.

It carries feeling

The speed and force of a mark are visible in thick paint. A face built from hard, decisive knife strokes reads very differently from one coaxed out with a soft brush, even if the likeness is the same.

A case in point

Zara Muse works only with palette knives, building women's faces from separate slabs of saturated acrylic. The texture is not decoration on top of the portrait; it is how the portrait is constructed. Her stated aim, to celebrate strength and resilience, is echoed in a surface that is literally built up and solid.

How to read a textured face

  1. Find where the paint is thickest. In most textured portraits it is on the lit side of the face: the brow, the cheekbone, the bridge of the nose. The painter is using real height to stand in for real light.
  2. Find where it is thinnest. Shadows and backgrounds are often thin, sometimes barely covering the ground. The contrast between thick and thin is doing as much work as the contrast between light and dark.
  3. Follow the direction of the strokes. Do they run with the form, wrapping round the cheek, or against it? Strokes that follow the form make a face feel solid; strokes that cut across it make it feel built or fractured.
  4. Look for what was left alone. Many painters leave the eyes or mouth smoother than the rest, so the viewer's attention settles there. Where the texture stops is as telling as where it is.
Try itPhotograph a textured portrait twice on your phone, once with the flash on and once with the room lights only, standing to one side. Compare the two. The flash picture shows the image; the side-lit picture shows the painting. Neither is wrong, and the gap between them is what texture adds.

The same structure, dark beneath and light built up on top, is explained stroke by stroke in Understanding palette-knife painting.

Caring for textured workThick paint collects dust in its ridges and can be damaged by careless handling. Hang it away from direct sun and radiators, dust only with a soft, dry brush, and never wipe it with a cloth.

articles.title: How to look at a painting in ten minutes
articles.dek: A simple method for standing in front of any painting and seeing more than you did a minute ago. No art history required.
articles.credit: Image: a visitor in front of a painting. [Image to supply]
articles.body:
Most people spend a few seconds in front of a painting, read the label, and move on. That is not a failing; nobody is taught how to look. This is a method you can use on any painting, in a gallery or on a screen, that takes about ten minutes and gets better with practice.

Minute one: stand back

Start further away than feels natural, far enough that you take in the whole canvas at once. Notice what you see first. Where does your eye land, and where does it go next? Painters plan this route, consciously or not, and the order in which you notice things is part of the work.

Minutes two and three: name what is there

Say to yourself, plainly, what is in the picture. A woman, turned slightly to the left, against a dark ground. Three slabs of orange where the cheek is. A horizon a third of the way up. This sounds too simple to be useful, but putting things into words forces you to see them, and you will notice details that a glance skipped.

Minutes four and five: step in close

Now go as close as the gallery allows and look at the surface rather than the image. Is the paint thick or thin? Can you see individual marks, and if so what made them: a soft brush, a stiff one, a knife, a finger? Are the edges between colours hard or soft? Where is the paint thickest, and is that also where the light falls in the picture? With a textured painting this is where most of the information lives.

Try itPick one small area, about the size of your palm, and count the separate marks in it. Then step back and see what those marks become from a distance. The gap between the two is the painter's skill.

Minute six: follow the light

Find the brightest point in the painting and the darkest. Work out where the light is supposed to be coming from, and whether it is consistent. Then notice the real light in the room: is it falling on the painting from above, from the side, from a window? For heavily textured work the real light matters as much as the painted one, which is why the same canvas can look flat in a photograph and alive on a wall.

Minute seven: look at the colour

Rather than naming colours, look for relationships. Which colours sit next to each other, and what do they do to one another? A grey next to orange looks blue; the same grey next to blue looks warm. Painters use this constantly. Notice too how few colours there may be: many striking paintings are built from three or four.

Minute eight: read the label last

Only now read the title, date and medium. Does the title change what you see? A title can point you to something you missed, or deliberately say less than the picture does. Check the medium against what you saw up close; it is a good test of your looking.

Minutes nine and ten: ask one question

Finish by asking a single question you cannot answer from the painting alone, and write it down. Why that colour for the background? Why is the figure cut off at the edge? Who was this for? These questions are where research starts, and they are what the portfolios on this site are built to answer.

If you want to practise on a painter whose surface rewards close looking, start with Zara Muse, whose knife-built portraits change completely between three paces and three inches.

articles.title: Oil or acrylic: what the difference means for the person who owns it
articles.dek: The two paints that make most contemporary pictures behave differently in the studio, on the wall and over the decades. Here is what to know.
articles.credit: Image: tubes of oil and acrylic paint. [Image to supply]
articles.body:
When a label says oil on canvas or acrylic on canvas, it is telling you more than a recipe. The two paints are made differently, handle differently and age differently, and a collector who knows the difference can look after a work properly and ask the right questions before buying.

What they are

Both are pigment, the coloured powder, held in a binder. In oil paint the binder is a drying oil, usually linseed, which hardens slowly by reacting with the air. In acrylic the binder is a plastic emulsion in water, which dries as the water leaves it. That one difference explains almost everything else.

In the studio

  • Time. Oil stays workable for hours or days, so colours can be blended on the canvas long after they are laid down. Acrylic can be dry to the touch in minutes, which suits painters who build up many layers in one session, and punishes anyone who wants to go back and soften an edge.
  • Thickness. Both can be laid on thickly. Heavy oil takes a very long time to dry right through and can wrinkle or crack if thick layers are rushed. Heavy-body acrylics and gel mediums are made to hold a peak, which is one reason many knife painters work in acrylic. Zara Muse, for instance, works in acrylic with knives and spatulas.[ap-muse]
  • Colour. Oil colours tend to dry close to how they look wet. Acrylic colours often dry a little darker, because the milky binder turns clear as it dries.

On the wall

A finished oil painting usually has a slightly softer, deeper surface, and is often varnished, which saturates the colour and protects it. Acrylic has a more even, sometimes slightly plastic sheen, and is less often varnished. In practice, with a textured painting, the difference is hard to see from across a room; close up, oil tends to show finer gradations within a single stroke.

Over the years

  • Oil continues to harden for decades. Old oil paintings can yellow slightly as the linseed oil ages, and thick passages can develop fine cracks. Both are normal and both can be treated by a conservator.
  • Acrylic stays flexible, which protects it from cracking, but the surface remains very slightly soft for life and attracts dust more readily. It also dislikes cold: below about ten degrees acrylic can become brittle, so never store an acrylic painting in an unheated garage or loft.

Looking after either

  • Hang away from direct sunlight, radiators and bathrooms. Steady, moderate temperature and humidity matter more than anything else.
  • Dust with a soft, dry brush, never a cloth, and never anything damp. On textured work, dust settles in the ridges; a soft brush lifts it out.
  • Do not try to clean, varnish or repair a painting yourself. Ask the gallery to recommend a conservator.
  • When moving a painting, carry it by the frame or stretcher, face towards you, and never let anything touch the painted surface.
Questions to ask before you buyWhat is the paint, exactly? What is it on: stretched canvas, board, paper? Has it been varnished? Any of these answers is fine; what you want is a gallery that knows and tells you.

articles.title: A short glossary of paint, from impasto to sgraffito
articles.dek: Twelve words that turn up in artist statements, labels and reviews, explained in plain English with a note on where to spot each one.
articles.body:
Art writing leans on a small vocabulary of technical terms, most of them borrowed from Italian or French. They are not difficult, but nobody explains them. Here are the ones you are most likely to meet, with what to look for in the painting itself.

About the paint

Pigment is the coloured powder. Binder is what holds it together and sticks it to the surface: oil, acrylic emulsion, egg in tempera, gum in watercolour. Medium has two meanings: the type of paint in general (oil is a medium) or a substance added to paint to change how it handles (a gel medium thickens acrylic). Context tells you which.

About the surface

Support is whatever the painting is on: canvas, linen, board, paper. Ground is the preparation layer, usually white or tinted, that seals the support and gives the paint something to hold. A coloured ground sometimes shows through at the edges of strokes; look for it between marks.

About the marks

Impasto is paint laid on thickly enough to stand up from the surface and cast its own shadow. Knife painters work almost entirely in impasto. Look at the painting from the side to see how high it is.

Glaze is the opposite: a thin, transparent layer of colour over dry paint beneath, which changes the colour below without hiding it. Old Master flesh and deep reds are built from glazes. Look for depth that seems to sit below the surface.

Scumble is a thin, broken layer of opaque or semi-opaque paint dragged over a dry layer so the lower colour shows through in patches. It gives a soft, hazy effect, often in skies and backgrounds.

Wet-in-wet (or alla prima, meaning at first attempt) is painting into paint that is still wet, so colours blend on the canvas. Wet-over-dry is the reverse. Most paintings use both; a hard edge usually means dry beneath, a soft one usually means wet.

Sgraffito is scratching through a wet layer to reveal the colour underneath, with the end of a brush, a knife edge or a tool. Look for fine lines that are lighter or darker than their surroundings and have a slightly ploughed edge.

About the whole picture

Palette is both the board the painter mixes on and the range of colours chosen for a work. A limited palette uses few colours; many strong paintings use three or four. Tonal range is the span from lightest to darkest. A painting with a narrow tonal range feels quiet; a wide one feels dramatic.

Try itTake any painting on this site, or any in a gallery, and find three of these in it. Impasto, a hard edge and a soft edge are usually the easiest to start with.

For how these marks work together in a face, read The role of texture in contemporary portraiture, and for the knife in particular, Understanding palette-knife painting.

articles.title: What is an art intervention?
articles.dek: When the artwork is an event in a public place rather than an object on a wall, how do you look at it, and what are you buying if you buy one?
articles.credit: Image: ANTI-FRIEZE, London, 2025. Courtesy Konn Artiss
articles.body:
An intervention is an artwork that interrupts a place or a situation that was not expecting it: a street, a fair, an auction, a museum. It is usually unannounced, usually temporary, and usually aimed at the people and institutions that happen to be there. The work is not only the object; it is the object, the place, the moment and the reaction, taken together.

Where the idea comes from

Artists have used public space to answer back to institutions for a long time. The Guerrilla Girls, an anonymous group of women artists, formed in 1985 in response to a Museum of Modern Art exhibition that featured only thirteen women among 169 artists,[tate-gg] and took to the streets of New York in gorilla masks with posters that counted how few women the museums were showing.[whitney-gg] The posters were cheap, temporary and pasted up at night. They are now in Tate's collection.[tate-gg]

The best-known recent intervention happened inside an auction. In October 2018 a Banksy canvas, Girl with Balloon, shredded itself in its frame moments after selling at Sotheby's in London.[tan-banksy] The half-shredded work was authenticated as a new piece, retitled Love is in the Bin, and sold again in 2021 for a record £18.5 million.[npr-banksy] Whatever Banksy intended, the market absorbed the joke and raised the price.

How to look at one

  • Ask where it happened and why there. The site is part of the work. Ice blocks outside an art fair mean something different from the same blocks in a park.
  • Ask who it addresses. Passers-by, the institution, the press, or collectors? Many interventions are made to be photographed and shared, so the audience is partly online.
  • Ask what is left afterwards. Photographs, video, a printed object, a puddle. What survives is often what ends up for sale.
  • Notice the timing. Interventions are usually timed to an event they comment on. Timing is a material like any other.

A current example

During Frieze week in October 2025, Konn Artiss placed blocks of ice holding effigies of famous artists outside Frieze London[ap-antifrieze] and further blocks outside galleries and auction houses in the city.[tan-frieze] Applying the questions above: the site was the market's own doorstep; the audience was the people arriving to buy; what survives is photographs and press; and the timing was the one week when the London market is most visible. Our review looks at how well it worked.

If you want to own one

You cannot buy a melted block of ice, but artists have long found ways to make temporary work collectable: a signed photograph or video, a printed edition, an object used in the piece, or a certificate that allows the work to be re-staged. Each is a different thing. Before buying, ask exactly which you are getting, how many exist, and whether the artist or their representative has authenticated it. The questions are the same as for any print; see Original, limited edition or open print?

A note on reportingInterventions are often first reported by the artists themselves, through press releases and social media. Where a claim about one has not been confirmed by an independent witness or publication, we mark it Reported.

articles.title: How prints are made: screenprint, etching, lithograph and giclée
articles.dek: Four very different processes share the word print. Knowing which one made the thing on your wall tells you how to value it and how to care for it.
articles.credit: Image: a screenprinting squeegee. [Image to supply]
articles.body:
Print covers everything from a hand-pulled etching to a poster from a shop. The processes below are the ones you will meet most often in contemporary galleries. For each, the question that matters is whether the artist made the image in the process itself, or whether the process reproduced an image made elsewhere.

Screenprint (silkscreen, serigraph)

Ink is pushed through a fine mesh screen with a squeegee, one colour at a time, with a stencil blocking the areas that should stay clear. Each colour needs its own screen and its own pass, so a print with twelve colours has been through the press twelve times. The result is flat, solid, saturated colour with crisp edges. Look for slight misregistration where one colour meets another, and for the very faint texture of the mesh in large flat areas. Pop art made the screenprint famous; it remains the most common original print process in contemporary editions.

Etching and other intaglio prints

A metal plate is coated with a waxy ground; the artist draws through the ground with a needle; acid bites the exposed lines into the metal. Ink is pushed into the lines, the surface wiped clean, and damp paper pressed onto the plate under great pressure. The paper picks up the ink from the grooves. Look for a plate mark, the slight rectangular dent around the image where the plate pressed into the paper, and for lines that stand very slightly proud of the surface because the ink was pulled up out of the grooves. Drypoint, aquatint and mezzotint are variations with different textures.

Lithograph

Based on the fact that grease and water repel each other. The artist draws on a flat stone or metal plate with a greasy crayon or ink; the surface is treated so the drawn areas accept printing ink and the blank areas, kept damp, refuse it. Lithographs can hold very fine tonal gradations, much like a drawing, which is what they often look like. Look for a soft, grainy quality in the tones and no plate mark.

Giclée and other digital prints

A high-resolution photograph or scan of an existing work is printed with pigment inks on archival paper or canvas. Giclée is a trade name that simply means a fine inkjet print. These are reproductions rather than original prints: the image was made first as a painting, and the printer's job is to match it. Quality varies enormously with the inks, the paper and the care taken in colour matching. Some are hand-finished by the artist with real paint, varnish or embellishment, which adds a layer that is unique to each sheet. Look at a light area through a magnifier: a very fine spray of dots rather than solid ink means digital.

What this means for value and care

  • An original print, where the artist worked in the process, is generally valued above a reproduction of the same image, edition sizes being equal. Neither is a lesser thing to own, provided it was sold as what it is.
  • Edition size and signature matter in both cases. Signed limited editions should come with paperwork that states the size; Zara Muse's editions through Grove Gallery, for example, are signed and come with a certificate of authenticity from the artist.[grove-zm]
  • All prints on paper want the same care: out of direct sun, framed with acid-free materials and ultraviolet-filtering glass, kept dry. Canvas prints are hardier but still fade in sunlight.
Try itNext time you are in a gallery or print room, look at the edge of a print's image for a plate mark, at a flat colour for mesh texture, and at a pale area through your phone camera zoomed in for a dot pattern. Three looks, three processes identified.

For how to read the numbers in the margin and what AP and PP mean, see Original, limited edition or open print?

articles.title: How to research an emerging artist
articles.dek: Where to look, what to ask, and which claims to check for yourself before you buy.
articles.body:
With an established artist, much of the research has been done for you by museums, critics and auction records. With an emerging artist, you have to do more of it yourself. That is not a reason to avoid new work; it is a reason to be methodical.

1. Start with the work

Before any research, decide whether you want to live with the piece. Look at as much of the artist's work as you can find. Is there a consistent voice? Does it develop over time, or repeat one successful idea? A clear, recognisable approach is a good sign; so is evidence of growth.

2. Build a timeline

Put together a simple career timeline: training, first exhibitions, notable sales, press. Then check each entry. An exhibition should be listed by the venue itself, not just in the artist's CV. A portfolio on World Art Review shows which facts we have confirmed and which are still awaiting a source, and you can apply the same discipline yourself.

3. Weigh the press

Not all coverage is equal. Independent reviews by critics and established art publications carry more weight than features based on press releases, and much more than paid or sponsored content. Ask of every article: who wrote it, did they see the work, and did anyone pay for it to appear?

4. Read auction results carefully

A strong auction result is real evidence of demand on that day, from at least two bidders. It is not a market on its own. Check the result on the auction house's own website, note whether the price includes the buyer's premium, and look for whether other works by the artist have sold, failed to sell or been withdrawn.

5. Understand what you are buying

  • Is it an original, a limited edition or an open edition print? See our guide to originals and prints.
  • For editions: how many in total, which number is yours, and are there artist's proofs on top?
  • Does it come with a certificate of authenticity, and who issued it?

6. Ask the gallery

A good gallery will answer these questions willingly and in writing: how long they have worked with the artist, what the artist's price history is, where the work has been exhibited, and what paperwork comes with it.

Red flagsPressure to decide quickly. Promises of guaranteed returns. Exhibition histories you cannot verify. Press coverage that turns out to be paid placement. None of these alone proves a problem, but each deserves a direct question.

articles.title: Original, limited edition or open print?
articles.dek: What each one is, how they are priced, how to read the numbers in the margin and how to tell them apart.
articles.body:
The same image can reach you in very different forms, at very different prices. Knowing which one you are looking at is the first thing to settle, and it is not always obvious from a photograph online.

Original

A unique work made by the artist's hand: a painting, drawing or sculpture. There is only one, which is why originals sit at the top of an artist's price range. With heavily textured work the difference is physical as well as legal: a knife-painted original has ridges you can see from the side, and a print of it is flat however good the printing.

Limited edition print

A fixed number of prints, each numbered and usually signed. Once the edition is sold, no more are made, and the smaller the edition the scarcer each print. Editions are made in two broad ways:

  • Original prints, such as screenprints, etchings and lithographs, where the artist makes the image on the screen, plate or stone and each sheet is pulled from it. The print is the artwork.
  • Reproductions, often called giclée prints, where a painting is photographed and printed with pigment inks on paper or canvas. Some are hand-finished by the artist, which adds a unique layer of real paint.

Both can be worth collecting, but they are different things, and the gallery should tell you plainly which you are buying. As an example of how an edition is described, Grove Gallery lists Zara Muse's print of Malala Yousafzai as a signed ultra limited edition of ten.[grove-chis]

Reading the margin

  • 12/50 means the twelfth print of an edition of fifty. The number does not usually affect value; the edition size does.
  • AP (artist's proof) is a small number of extra prints kept by the artist, traditionally about ten per cent of the edition. They are often priced slightly higher.
  • PP (printer's proof) and HC (hors commerce, not for sale) are further proofs outside the numbered run. Ask how many exist in total.
  • A pencil signature and number in the lower margin is the convention for works on paper. Canvas editions are usually signed on the front or back.

Open edition print

A reproduction with no fixed limit. These are the most affordable way to own an image you love, but they are not scarce and are rarely bought with resale in mind. There is nothing wrong with them as long as they are sold as what they are.

How to tell

  • Look for a number and signature. If there is no number, assume it is open edition until told otherwise.
  • Ask for the edition size, how it was printed, and whether any proofs exist beyond the numbered run.
  • Check whether a certificate states the edition details and who issued it. Signed Zara Muse editions, for instance, come with a certificate of authenticity from the artist.[grove-zm]
  • For originals, look for surface texture and visible marks of the hand. Ask for a photograph taken in raking light from the side.
Caring for printsKeep works on paper out of direct sun, frame them with acid-free mounts and glass that filters ultraviolet light, and never trim the margins: the signature and number are part of the work.

articles.title: Provenance and certificates, explained
articles.dek: The paperwork that should travel with a work, what a certificate can and cannot prove, and why it matters when you come to insure or sell.
articles.body:
Provenance is the history of who has owned a work since it left the artist's studio. A certificate of authenticity is a document stating that a work is genuine. Together they are the work's passport, and like a passport they are only as good as whoever issued them.

What good paperwork includes

  • Artist's name, title, date, medium and dimensions
  • For prints, the edition size, this print's number and the total number of proofs
  • Who issued the certificate, with a signature and a date
  • An invoice showing where and when you bought it, and for how much
  • Any exhibition history, with venue names and dates

What a certificate proves, and what it does not

A certificate signed by the artist, or issued by the artist's studio or the gallery that represents them, is strong evidence. A certificate from a third party who never handled the work, or a generic card with no issuer named, proves very little. If the artist is living, the best confirmation is the simplest: the artist or their gallery confirming in writing that the work is theirs.

The chain of ownership

For a new work bought directly from the artist's gallery, provenance is short: studio, gallery, you. Keep it that way by keeping the invoice. For a work bought second-hand, ask for the previous owner's paperwork too. Gaps are not unusual, but a gap at the start, with no record of where the work first came from, is where most problems begin.

Why it matters

Insurers, auction houses and future buyers will all ask for it. A work with a clear, documented history is easier to insure, easier to sell and more likely to hold its value. For prints, the paperwork is often the only way to tell a legitimate edition from an unauthorised copy.

Keep a file

Keep certificates, invoices, exhibition labels, correspondence with the gallery and good photographs of each work together, on paper and as scans. Photograph the front, the back, the signature and any labels on the frame. Add a photograph of the work hanging in your home, which insurers like, and note any conservation work with dates.

If something is missingAsk the gallery to reissue a certificate or confirm the sale in writing. Most will. If they cannot or will not, that is useful information in itself.

articles.title: Mixed-media art: materials, meaning and conservation
articles.dek: When ice, print and found objects become the artwork, what are you looking at, and what are you buying?
articles.body:
Mixed media simply means a work made from more than one material. That can be as gentle as a painting with collaged paper, or as far-reaching as an installation of ice, effigies and printed newspapers. What links them is that the choice of material is part of the meaning.

Four words you will meet

Collage is flat material, usually paper or fabric, glued to a surface. Assemblage is the three-dimensional version, objects fixed together into a sculpture. Installation is work that takes over a space, so that the room itself is part of the piece. Ephemeral describes work made to last only a short time, whether that is ice, flowers, chalk or a performance. A single work can be all four at once.

Reading materials as meaning

Ask why each material is there. Newspaper suggests news, opinion and disposability. Found objects bring their own history into the work. Ice is the most extreme example: it exists only for as long as the weather allows. When Konn Artiss sealed effigies of famous artists in blocks of ice outside Frieze London, the melting was the point.[ap-antifrieze]

Try itStanding in front of any mixed-media work, list every material you can identify, then for each one ask two questions: where did it come from before it was art, and what would change if the artist had used something else? If the answer to the second question is "nothing", the material is probably there for how it looks. If the work would mean something different, the material is part of the message.

The conservation problem

Different materials age at different speeds. Paper yellows and becomes brittle, especially if it is acidic. Glues fail. Plastics can discolour or become sticky. Fabrics fade. A mixed-media work can change unevenly, one part ageing while another stays fresh.

  • Keep work out of direct sunlight, which fades paper, inks and textiles fastest.
  • Avoid damp and big swings in temperature, which stress joins between materials.
  • Ask the artist or gallery what materials were used, and keep that list.
  • Use a conservator who handles mixed media, not a general picture restorer.

Collecting work that is meant to disappear

Some works are not meant to last at all. Artists have long found ways around this: a certificate that authorises the work to be remade, written instructions, or a related object such as a print, photograph or edition. If you are offered a work connected to a temporary piece, ask exactly what you own: the object in front of you, the right to remake something, or a record of an event.

For how to look at temporary public work as a whole, and what collectors have historically bought from it, read What is an art intervention?

articles.title: ANTI-FRIEZE: what melts when the art market is put on ice
articles.dek: During Frieze week, blocks of ice holding effigies of famous artists appeared outside the fair and London's auction houses. What does the work say about value, and what is left once the ice has gone?
articles.credit: Image: ANTI-FRIEZE, London, October 2025. Courtesy Konn Artiss
articles.body:
Frieze week is when London's art market is at its most confident: the fair, the auctions and the gallery openings all pulling in the same direction. In October 2025, Konn Artiss chose that week to put the market on ice.

The work

Outside Frieze London stood five large blocks of ice, each holding an effigy of an artist whose name is now a brand: Damien Hirst, Andy Warhol, Tracey Emin, Jeff Koons and KAWS.[ap-antifrieze] Elsewhere in the city, further blocks appeared outside major galleries and auction houses, including one beside a framed image at Phillips.[tan-frieze]

What it says

The joke lands quickly. These are artists whose work is collected, stored, insured and preserved as carefully as any asset, and here they are frozen solid, in public, with no one to keep them cold. The longer argument takes the whole week to make. As the ice melts, what is left is water, debris and a crowd of people who stopped to watch. Value, the work suggests, is a kind of attention, and attention melts too.

Does it work?

As a piece of timing and staging, yes. It is legible in seconds, photographs well and makes a clear point in a place where that point is hardest to ignore. The weaker side is that critique of the art market made during Frieze week is itself very good publicity, and the project benefits from the attention it mocks. That tension is probably deliberate. It is also worth noticing.

VerdictA sharp, well-timed intervention that is better at asking its question than answering it. Worth knowing as a marker of how contemporary artists are using spectacle to talk back to the market.

articles.title: The Washington Ghost: satire as a printed newspaper
articles.dek: Ten thousand copies, handed out in Venice. Is a newspaper an artwork?
articles.credit: Image: The Washington Ghost, Venice, 2025. [Image to supply]
articles.body:
Before Jeff Bezos's wedding in Venice in June 2025, more than 10,000 copies of a satirical newspaper called The Washington Ghost were distributed in the city, credited to Konn Artiss.[gb-venice]

A newspaper as a medium

The form is the cleverest part. A newspaper looks like information, costs nothing and is designed to be thrown away. Putting satire into that format lets the work move through a city the way news does, hand to hand, without a gallery or a ticket. It also borrows the name and look of a famous newspaper owned by the very person it mocks, which sharpens the joke.

What survives

Most copies will have been binned within a day. The ones that remain become something else: a document of an event, and possibly a collectable. That shift, from free giveaway to object with value, is exactly the process the artist's later work at Frieze makes fun of.

Note on sourcesFAD Magazine reports that related work was displayed at the National Portrait Gallery in Washington.[fad-ghost] We have not confirmed this independently.

articles.title: Zara Muse and Konn Artiss: two ways to talk about value
articles.dek: One builds it into the paint. The other lets it melt on the pavement.
articles.body:
Put side by side, these two artists could hardly look more different. Zara Muse makes solid, textured portraits meant to hang on a wall for decades. Konn Artiss makes interventions that are designed to vanish within days. Yet both are, in their own way, talking about value.

Permanence and its opposite

Muse's paintings are about building up: layer after layer of paint, a career built from a personal turning point, portraits of women chosen for their strength.[ap-muse] Artiss's work is about things falling apart: frozen effigies of famous artists left to melt, newspapers made to be thrown away.[ap-antifrieze]

What each asks of you

A Muse painting asks you to slow down and look closely at a surface. An Artiss intervention asks you to notice the system around the art: who is famous, who is paid, who controls the street. Reading them together is a useful reminder that contemporary art covers both: the made object and the questions about why objects are valued at all.
